sections.h2: What is the Illinois transfer tax on a home sale?
sections.html:
Illinois taxes the privilege of transferring title to real estate at 50 cents for each $500 of value, or fraction of $500, stated in the transfer declaration (35 ILCS 200/31-10). The tax applies to deeds, to beneficial interests in a land trust and to controlling interests in a real estate entity. It is due whether or not a document is ever recorded, and it covers transfers made through several related transactions.

Counties may add a second layer and a few cities add a third. For a seller in Illinois, the number on the closing statement is therefore the state stamp plus whatever the county and municipality charge. Chicago is the best known example of a city layer,.

The statute leaves the split between buyer and seller to the parties. Your purchase contract and the title company decide who covers the state and county stamps, so read that clause before you sign.

sections.h2: How do the state, county and Chicago layers compare?
sections.html:
The three layers use the same unit, a block of $500 of value, but the rate per block differs. The table shows only rates as the official pages print them.

Transfer tax layers in Illinois, per $500 of value or fraction. Sources: 35 ILCS 200/31-10, 55 ILCS 5/5-1031 and the City of Chicago Department of Finance.
LayerRateWho sets it
State of Illinois50 centsProperty Tax Code, Article 31
County (optional)25 centsCounty board, if it adopts the tax
City of Chicago, City portion$3.75Municipal Code chapter 3-33
City of Chicago, CTA portion$1.50Municipal Code chapter 3-33
City of Chicago, combined$5.25Buyer generally owes $3.75, seller $1.50

The county tax comes from 55 ILCS 5/5-1031. It is collected by the recorder or registrar of titles before the deed is recorded, and it sits on top of every other privilege tax imposed by the state or a municipality. Ask the county recorder whether your county has adopted it.

sections.h2: Who collects the tax, and when is it paid?
sections.html:
The county recorder or registrar of titles collects the state tax. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-15, paper revenue stamps were to be phased out by December 31, 2025, and counties now issue electronic stamps or another electronic mark. Each recorder files a return with the Department of Revenue and remits the money by the 10th of the following month.

A deed cannot be accepted for recording until the stamps in the right amount have been bought, unless the deed is exempt. The recorder may affix the stamp before or after recording at the grantee's request. Ask your closing agent how the stamps are ordered and paid from the settlement funds.

  • The tax is computed from the value stated on the declaration, not from the assessed value on the tax bill.
  • The declaration goes to the recorder with the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer, whichever comes first.
  • The Department of Revenue's MyDec system accepts the state forms and Chicago's Form 7551. Counties outside MyDec use fill-in PDF forms.

sections.h2: Which Illinois transfers are exempt from the state transfer tax?
sections.html:
Section 31-45 lists the exempt deeds, and several of them matter to sellers in distress. A deed issued to a mortgage holder in a foreclosure, or in a transfer in lieu of foreclosure, is exempt, and so is a tax deed. The exemption list also covers deeds that secure a debt, deeds that release a security interest and deeds of partition. Some exempt transfers still require the declaration to be filed.

  • Deeds where the actual consideration is under $100.
  • Deeds that confirm, correct or supplement a deed already on record, with no added consideration.
  • Transfers to or from governmental bodies and certain charitable, religious or educational organizations, which must still file the declaration.
  • Real estate swaps, except that any cash difference between the properties is taxable.
  • Home purchases by participants in the Home Ownership Made Easy program, which also still file the declaration.

An exemption does not apply by default. The deed or the declaration has to cite the exemption that fits. Ask the recorder how your county wants the exemption notation written.

sections.h2: What does Form PTAX-203 ask a seller to report?
sections.html:
Form PTAX-203, the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, must be signed by at least one seller and one buyer or their agents. The Department of Revenue uses the answers for sales ratio studies that feed the state equalization factors, so the form asks for more than the price.

  • The full actual consideration, excluding credits or refunds for repairs and improvements.
  • Personal property in the sale. An itemized list is required when personal property on a residence exceeds 5 percent of the price.
  • Whether the buyer will use the home as a principal residence, and whether the house was sold through an agent or advertised.
  • Special circumstances such as a court-ordered sale (including probate and foreclosure), a short sale, a bank-owned resale or a seller or buyer that is a financial institution.
  • Homestead exemptions shown on the most recent tax bill.

Willfully falsifying or leaving out required information is a Class B misdemeanor for a first offense under the Department's instructions. A buyer who knowingly gives a false grantee identity in Cook County faces its own misdemeanor charge. Sellers should check the form for accuracy before signing, even when the title company prepares it.

sections.h2: How does the Chicago transfer tax work for a seller?
sections.html:
Chicago imposes its tax on transferring title or a beneficial interest in real property in the city, whether or not the contract was signed in Chicago. The official page for Form 7551 gives $3.75 per $500 for the City portion and $1.50 per $500 for the CTA portion on transfers on or after April 1, 2008, for a combined $5.25. In general the buyer is responsible for $3.75 and the seller for $1.50.

The Department of Finance page lists exemptions that include transfers to lenders in foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure, tax deeds, deeds securing debt, transfers under $500, and a court-ordered transfer of a primary residence between members of a couple in a divorce or legal separation. No transfer is exempt unless the declaration describes the facts and attaches support.

A refund of the CTA portion is available to a transferee who is 65 or older, occupies the home as a personal dwelling for at least a year, and bought at $250,000 or less. That refund is claimed by the buyer through the Tax Division, so it does not change what a Chicago seller owes.

sections.h2: How do mortgages, probate and as-is sales affect the tax?
sections.html:
When the deed says the property is transferred subject to a mortgage, the outstanding balance is left out of the tax basis. The PTAX-203 handles this with a separate line for the mortgage amount to which the property remains subject, so the figure on the deed matters. Ask your closing attorney which wording fits your sale.

A sale from an estate follows the same stamp rules as any other sale. The form has a box for court-ordered sales that covers probate, and the personal representative signs as seller. A lender that takes title by foreclosure deed or deed in lieu pays no state stamp. The lender's later resale is an ordinary sale and is reported on the form's bank REO line.

Selling as is does not change the tax. The price on the declaration is the price actually paid, and repair credits given to the buyer are excluded from it. Keep the written credit in the closing file, because the Department's instructions refer to amounts credited against the price for repairs.

sections.h2: What should an Illinois seller do before closing?
sections.html:
Treat the transfer tax as one more line to confirm early, not a surprise at the closing table.

  • Ask the county recorder whether a county transfer tax applies and what the recording office accepts as proof of exemption.
  • Confirm with the title company who pays each layer under your contract.
  • Review the draft PTAX-203, especially the price, the personal property line and any special-circumstance boxes.
  • If the house is in Chicago, ask for the Form 7551 total and the buyer and seller shares.
  • Keep a copy of the signed declaration with your closing papers.

A cash buyer that purchases a house as is can sign the same declaration and use the same recorder, so the transfer tax steps stay identical whether you list or sell directly.

faqs.q: What is the Illinois state transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: It is 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500 stated in the declaration, under 35 ILCS 200/31-10. Counties may add 25 cents per $500, and Chicago adds its own tax.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax in Illinois?
faqs.a: The statute does not assign it, so the purchase contract and local custom decide. In Chicago the city's official page says the buyer is generally responsible for $3.75 and the seller for $1.50 per $500.

faqs.q: Is a foreclosure or tax deed subject to the transfer tax?
faqs.a: No. Deeds issued to a mortgage holder in foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure, and tax deeds, are exempt under 35 ILCS 200/31-45. The declaration is still part of the recording process unless the deed qualifies for a notation only.

faqs.q: When must the transfer declaration be filed?
faqs.a: It must be presented with the deed at recording, or within 3 business days after the transfer, whichever is earlier. A deed without the declaration is not accepted for recording unless an exemption applies.

faqs.q: How are transfer tax stamps issued now?
faqs.a: Paper revenue stamps were to be phased out by December 31, 2025, so counties issue electronic stamps or other electronic indicia. Ask your county recorder how the stamp appears on the recorded deed.
